entries.title: Complaints Against DOJ Officials Have Surged During Trump’s Second Term
entries.summary: The Office of Professional Responsibility has seen a 54% increase in misconduct complaints over the last two years, an inspector general report found.
entries.content:
Professional misconduct complaints against Department of Justice personnel have surged during President Donald Trump’s second term, according to an annual inspector general report documenting the department’s top challenges.

Tuesday’s findings from the department’s independent oversight office follow last year’s workforce reductions and a record-high caseload that includes dozens of lawsuits against the president’s political opponents.

The high number of complaints have led the department to open investigations into attorney misconduct, whistleblower retaliation and federal law enforcement conduct violations, the report says.

The DOJ’s Office of Professional Responsibility reported receiving 2,081 professional misconduct complaints last fiscal year, representing a 54% increase from 1,346 in 2024, the last full fiscal year during then-President Joe Biden’s administration, the report says.

The administration has been quickly outpacing DOJ complaints filed during Biden’s tenure, which were at their lowest in fiscal year 2023 at 1,085 recorded complaints, and their highest in 2024.

OPR found professional misconduct in each of the nine full-scale investigations that it completed this year, while one additional investigation has not yet been concluded, the report says. The office also received 50 new FBI whistleblower retaliation complaints.

The inspector general noted that the surge in misconduct complaints has put strain on the department’s shrinking workforce.

“These results demonstrate that OPR has continued to resolve substantial workloads despite its limited size,” the report states. “However, the Department faces risk in its oversight capacity if OPR’s staffing levels are insufficient to manage the workload generated by the Department’s thousands of employees.”

The review coincides with a record number of staff departures at the Department of Justice. The report cites a net decline of 10,345 department employees between January 2025 and May 2026.

Staffing levels are also impacting federal prosecutors’ ability to try cases across the country.

The report acknowledged concerns over the loss of critical expertise across the department, noting a 40% vacancy rate in the Missing or Murdered Indigenous Persons Regional Outreach Program and sprawling staffing issues in the Bureau of Prisons.

“Workforce reductions may produce mission degradation that aggregate staffing numbers do not reveal, particularly where departures are concentrated in specialized or difficult-to-replace positions,” the report warned.
entries.author: Gavin J. Quinton

entries.title: The Final Senate Race Is Called: Mary Peltola Flips Alaska Seat
entries.summary: The outcome of the race will give Democrats 56 seats in the Senate next year.
entries.content:
Mary Peltola is projected to win her race for U.S. Senate over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, locking in a Democratic Senate majority in which the party will hold 56 seats.

Alaska was the final Senate race left to be called, and took two weeks to conclude: On Tuesday evening, Peltola broke a majority of votes cast, meaning the contest didn’t require additional ranked-choice tabulations.

The weeks leading up to and after the election were marked by a flurry of legal activity around the contest.

Less than two weeks out from Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit that teed up a legal challenge to a possible Peltola victory. The lawsuit against Alaska election officials argued that they should not certify any outcome “that may be impacted by voter confusion” between Sen. Sullivan, the incumbent, and Daniel J. Sullivan, another candidate who appeared on the four-person ballot, without an investigation.

A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit, which was widely panned as a nonstarter by legal experts, the Sunday before Election Day. Democrats, including Peltola’s campaign, condemned the federal lawsuit but weren’t the only ones: Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska said the Justice Department “should never have filed this lawsuit,” in a clear break from her Republican peers.

The DOJ’s lawsuit divided Alaska’s state officials, too: While Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy said he would not commit to certifying the race results if there was uncertainty about the outcome, attorneys for Alaska election officials argued in a filing that a federal challenge to certifying the results has “no legal basis.” The chief officer of the Alaska Division of Elections is Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom, a Republican.

Just a week before Election Day, The New York Times reported that the Peltola campaign and national Democrats had plotted to recruit spoiler candidates to siphon votes from Sen. Sullivan — including Daniel J. Sullivan, the subject of the legal battle between the DOJ and Alaska election officials. Both the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee denied involvement in the recruitment to The Washington Sun.

The New York Times’ reporting bolstered the DOJ’s legal challenge — attorneys filed an amended complaint drawing on the evidence of the plan a few days later. The news also prompted backlash from Republicans toward Democrats: President Donald Trump said in a Truth Social post that Peltola should face legal and political consequences. Three investigations kicked off days after the news broke: Alaska’s governor ordered state officials to look into the plot, House Republicans announced a probe and the DOJ sent target letters to several people involved.

Some prominent Democrats defended the Peltola campaign, and national Democrats including Maryland Rep. Jamie Raskin said candidate recruitment is a common campaign tactic. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) called the plan to recruit other candidates “pretty dumb” but also highlighted that the actions aren’t illegal, and that it “happens in every election.”

Although Murkowski criticized the DOJ’s lawsuit, she also called the reported plot “simply wrong.”

In the days after the election, Trump posted on Truth Social, arguing that votes for Daniel J. Sullivan and the fourth candidate should be counted for Sen. Sullivan, citing potential confusion on the part of voters, and calling the race “rigged.”

A separate lawsuit also kicked off after Election Day.

As part of Alaska’s tabulation process, ballots are reviewed and can be rejected if election officials find voter information invalid or questionable. Peltola’s campaign sued the Alaska Division of Elections on Nov. 7, seeking to force the government to reveal the names of voters whose absentee ballots were rejected, but a state judge dismissed this new lawsuit four days later.

The state judge told the campaign that its request was “unreasonable” given the limited time for election officials to tabulate ballots.

Peltola’s win marks a striking shift in the state given that Trump won Alaska by 13 percentage points in 2024 — the same year Peltola lost her at-large congressional seat to Republican Rep. Nick Begich.

The Alaska Senate race was a competitive one, with the affordability crisis and Iran war on voters’ minds. Peltola focused on an “Alaska First” message and hammered Trump’s handling of the economy and foreign affairs, especially the president’s hostility toward Canada. Peltola, who is a Yup’ik Alaska Native, will be the first Alaska Native U.S. senator.

The Democrat also got a boost from a national political environment that soured on Trump and Republicans more broadly.

“She fixed the campaign on Alaskan issues versus hyperpartisan national issues,” said John-Henry Heckendorn, a Democratic strategist. “That’s allowed her to pull together a coalition across party lines that could actually compete with MAGA.”
entries.author: Ellie Fivas
